title: NativeVoice — dictation that doesn’t stop at English
description: Mac dictation for people who don't dictate in English. Built on the ElevenLabs Scribe API. 36 languages, hold-to-talk, your own key, cents per use.
h1: Dictation that doesn’t stop at English.
lede: Hold a key, speak, let go — the text appears where your cursor is. Dictation on a Mac is excellent in English and patchy to absent in everything else. This is built the other way round.
why: Built on the ElevenLabs Scribe API. I tried the alternatives on the languages I actually dictate in, and this was the one that got them right — reliably, and accurately enough to trust. It costs cents.
meta: Free · open source · macOS 13+ · Apple silicon and Intel
shot.listening: The recording panel, showing the level while you speak
c1.p: Including the ones the big tools treat as minor. All of them behave the same — there is no first-class language here.
c2.p: Hold right Command, speak, let go. No window to learn, no mode to enter, nothing to click first.
c3.p: Your ElevenLabs key, stored in the macOS keychain and never shown again. You pay them directly for what you dictate.
c4.p: Names and jargon are what transcription gets wrong. A plain text file of your terms, read before every transcription.
c5.p: Audio is deleted as soon as it is transcribed. History is off until you turn it on, and switching it off deletes what was stored.
c6.p: MIT, about 3,500 lines, no dependencies. Signed and notarized, and it updates itself — never while you are dictating.
lang.sub: Including the ones the big tools treat as minor. macOS gives an offline model, automatic punctuation and continuous listening to en-US alone.
menu.sub: There is no settings window to go hunting through. What the app can do, it does from here — and what you see is all of it.
menu.p: Language, trigger key, recording cap and your vocabulary; sounds, automatic pasting and filler removal; your ElevenLabs usage against its limit; and the log, which explains in plain sentences what the app did and why.
setup.sub: Ten minutes. You bring your own ElevenLabs key: you pay them directly for what you dictate and nothing goes through anyone else. Their free tier is 10,000 credits a month and transcription costs 330 credits a minute — about half an hour of dictation every month for nothing. Check their current pricing before you rely on that.
s1: Drag NativeVoice into Applications and open it. It has no window; look for it in the menu bar.
s2: Make a key at ElevenLabs → Settings → API Keys and copy it at once — they show it only the first time.
s4: Say yes when it asks for the microphone, Input Monitoring and Accessibility. It raises the dialogs itself; you do not have to go looking.
s5: Let it restart when it offers. macOS hands Input Monitoring to a freshly started process only, so nothing works until it does.
foot.ai: Translated into thirty-five other languages by a machine that lives in none of them.
